BMJ 1984; 289: 51. Constipation The pattern of normal defaecation is extremely variable, which makes constipation hard to define, and to some ex- tent subjective. However, expert consensus considers that it occurs if 2 or more of the following features are present for at least 12 weeks in the previous year: less than 3 defaecations in a week, or hard or lumpy stool, straining, feeling of incomplete evacuation or anorectal blockage, or need for manual assistance, on at least a quarter of occa- sions.1 New onset constipation, especially in patients over 50 years of age, or accompanying symptoms such as anae- mia, abdominal pain, weight loss, or overt or occult blood in the stool should provoke urgent investigation because of the risk of malignancy or other serious bowel disorder.2-5 Constipation can be a symptom of a range of disorders or of drug toxicity2,5,6 and appropriate management of any underlying cause is required. It tends to be more common in the elderly
